name: Beth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on at 6:30 at the Canal Street Fresh supermarket, which is the big one by the old mill. I open a till, but as a team lead I also sort the rota swaps, count the safe and look after the new starters. The best part is my regulars, and the worst is standing nine hours with a bad back while the self-checkout beeps behind me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most by the end of a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The arguing with the machines, honestly. I spend half the day walking over to the self-checkouts to clear an unexpected item in the bagging area. It's a job that used to be four of us chatting with customers, and now it's one of me running between screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I've said for two years: the machines are mostly a way to trim hours, not a miracle. The self-checkouts already took four of our twelve tills. If AI is hype, I'd tell my friends it's the same old story with a shinier name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit relieved, but not safe. My hours fell from 38 to 31 last spring and the rent didn't fall with them. Dani (my partner) works at a care home on a low wage, so between us we have about two weeks of slack, never a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same job and keep going to the union meeting on the first Thursday. I'd say yes to every extra shift, because as a team lead I'm asked first. I'd cancel the gym and stop buying lunch, which saves me about thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. I love my regulars, like old Mr Alder who counts out his coins, and I like training the new starters. AI being hype doesn't stop the supermarket cutting our hours anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the self-checkouts already cost hours. What did that look like last spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In April they took a whole evening shift off the rota and called it "efficiency". I was short by about 140 that month and put the electric bill on a card. I told Dani we'd skip the weekend away, and she went quiet, which is worse than shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When hours get cut, who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and the head office, not the machines. Someone chose to put four tills in a corner and call it progress. I'd like a law that says a shop of our size has to keep a minimum number of staffed tills.

say: The **machines** are a way to trim hours, not a miracle, and the owners decide that.
I'd tell friends this is the **same old story** with a shinier name.
think: I feel a bit **relieved**, but not safe, because my hours already fell from 38 to 31.
Dani's care-home pay and mine leave only about **two weeks** of slack.
do: Keep taking **extra shifts** because team leads get asked first.
Cancel the gym and stop buying work lunches to save about **thirty a week**.
Go to the **union** meeting every first Thursday.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, and proud of my regulars.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't stop the supermarket cutting our hours anyway.
fieldNote: Hours were cut before any real AI: **self-checkouts** are her proof that hype still hurts.
Public line and private view match, apart from a **relief** she won't admit at work.
Blames owners and head office rather than technology, and wants a **staffing rule**.

steps.text: Take every extra shift the rota offers, starting with weekends
Cancel the gym and stop buying lunch at work
Attend the union meeting on the first Thursday each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say AI answering customers is fine until a customer wants a person, and then the queue is on us. I'd say the stock ordering and rota planning will go to software first. Friends would hear me say that the shop floor is where it hurts, because those are the jobs left to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the thinking tasks aren't my day. I scan, bag, fix mistakes and calm people down, and my other jobs are the rota and the cash count, which software could do. If head office moves those, they won't need a team lead, and I'd be back at base pay on a till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and ask the union to push for a say before new software goes in. I'd put 60 a month into a savings account and not touch it, which is a stretch on my wage. I won't be trying any AI tool, because I'd rather learn about it from the union than from a manager's training video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for a letter. I'm not scared today, but I know the rota software is coming and the team lead role is the easy bit to trim. My nan used to say you can't fight the weather, but you can bring a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which thinking tasks in your own day could software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they trialled software that writes the rota. It sent two of my single-mum colleagues the same Sunday shift twice and nobody at head office could explain why. I fixed it by hand and got no thanks for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger colleagues on the tills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to join the union now and keep their own record of their hours. A lot of them are 19 and think a till job is forever. Mine isn't a bad job, but I don't think it's forever either.

say: AI answering customers is fine until someone wants a **person**, and then the queue is ours.
Ordering and rota planning will go to software first, so **shop floor** jobs are what's left to cut.
think: My rota and cash-count work could go to software, and then nobody needs a **team lead**.
I'd be back at **base pay** on a till.
do: Ask the union to demand a **say** before new software arrives.
Save **60 a month** and leave it alone.
Avoid AI tools and learn through the **union** instead.
feel: Like **waiting** for a letter, calm today but braced for the team lead role to go.
S1.quote: Mine isn't a bad job, but I don't think it's forever either.
fieldNote: She places herself in the **desk-like** part of her work, rota and counts, which is the part software takes first.
Resistance to AI tools is **principled**, tied to union trust, not fear.
Wants worker **say** over rollout rather than to stop it.

steps.text: Push the union to demand a say before rota software goes live
Move 60 a month into a savings account untouched
Hold the team lead role and watch what head office trials next

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd be loud: two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd say the government has to act before the firms do, with wage support and a retraining fund. At the pub I'd say this is when a union either matters or doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. The thinking AI would run the ordering, the rota and the customer chat by 2028, so head office would need maybe a third of the managers. Then three years later the tills and shelf-stacking go to robots, and I'm 32 with no savings and few shops nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd drag every pound into savings and ask Dani to do the same. I'd go to the union and push for a deal that gives a redundancy payment, and I'd write to the local councillor about it. I'd also look at the community college for a care or nursing assistant course, because Dani says there's always a job in care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and a bit angry. I've been the best till worker in this shop for six years and a machine will get my badge. Being the best at a job that is about to vanish doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What changes in your day-to-day plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty-six months of grace isn't nothing, I suppose. The robots in the shop would still need someone to fix them and to deal with shoplifters, but I've seen the robot demo, and it was slow and kept dropping tins. Still, slow isn't the same as never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots would come around 2031. Does that comfort you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd have wasted the thirty-odd hours I've given the union if nobody listens. I don't trust the firm to look after me, so I want it in writing from the government.

say: Two years isn't enough, so **government** has to act before firms do, with wage support and retraining.
This is when a **union** either matters or doesn't.
think: Thinking AI would run ordering, rota and customer chat by 2028, and head office would need a **third** of its managers.
Robots take the tills about **three years** later, and I'd be 32 with no savings.
do: Put every spare pound into **savings** and get Dani to do the same.
Push the union for a **redundancy deal** and write to the local councillor.
Look at a **care assistant** course at the community college.
feel: **Alarmed** and angry, because being the best at a vanishing job doesn't pay rent.
S2.quote: Being the best at a job that is about to vanish doesn't pay the rent.
fieldNote: The **three-year** robot gap gives her little comfort: she sees the demo as slow, not never.
Turns fear into **organising** and politics, which fits her outlook.
Care work is her fallback, taken from **Dani's** world rather than any plan of her own.

steps.text: Put every spare pound into a savings account and ask Dani to match
Push the union for a redundancy deal and a retraining fund
Write to the local councillor demanding wage support
Ask the community college about a care assistant course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a window, so I'd say it plainly: use it. At work I'd tell the younger ones to save, learn something, and not wait for the firm. I'd also say employers should say what they're planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it's still frightening, but it's a fear with a calendar. By 2031 the thinking work is gone, and the robots reach the tills around 2034, when I'm 35. That's enough time to get a care qualification if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start one evening course a week in the first year, probably a health care assistant certificate. I'd keep the supermarket shifts through it and put the same 60 a month away. I'd also join the union committee, because I'd rather be in the room than reading the minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier than with two years. I'd feel like I was doing something, not just bracing. It still makes me sad, because I like this job and I'm good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do differently with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to tell us, in plain words, which jobs are going and when. If head office wants the tills to run with robots, they could pay for staff to train for the jobs that stay. A written plan and money for course fees would do more than any pep talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid study leave, even two hours a week. That's a cheap thing for a big firm and a huge thing for someone on my pay. If they said no, I'd take it to the union committee.

say: Five years is a **window**, so use it, and employers should say what they're planning now.
I'd tell the younger ones to **save** and learn something instead of waiting for the firm.
think: It's still frightening, but the fear now has a **calendar**: thinking work goes by 2031, robots reach tills around 2034.
That's enough time to get a **care qualification** if I start now.
do: Start a weekly evening **health care assistant** course in the first year.
Keep the shifts and the 60-a-month **savings** going.
Join the **union committee** to be in the room.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because doing something beats bracing.
S3.quote: A written plan and money for course fees would do more than any pep talk.
fieldNote: More time converts dread into a **plan**: the extra years are what make retraining believable.
Her ask of employers is concrete: **study leave** and a written plan.
Still sad about leaving a job she is **proud** of.

steps.text: Start a weekly evening health care assistant certificate course
Keep putting 60 a month into savings while studying
Join the union committee and ask for paid study leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost like a normal career plan. At work I'd say it's an argument for fixing things properly: training funds, and wage support, and unions at the table. I'd say it as a debate, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be mostly okay, but a little uneasy. By 2036 I'm 37, and that's a long runway to get a qualification and maybe even a house deposit. The risk is that people say there's plenty of time and then do nothing, and I count myself in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care course at a slower pace, then try for a better-paid role in a care home or clinic by about 2030. I'd keep working at the supermarket until I had a new job lined up. I'd save steadily and talk to Dani about moving to a smaller place with cheaper rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a nag in the back. Ten years of not being sure is its own strain, like living with a leak you can't find. But at least I'd have time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you want to have done by 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say by 2030 I want a qualification, a job offer and six months of rent saved. The rent bit is the hard part on my pay, so I'd probably set up a small automatic transfer. If I miss it I feel guilty, which is why automatic is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell younger people anything different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to them: don't stay on the tills just because you're good at it. Being good gets you a team lead badge, not a pension. Look at what the shop can't do without a person, like helping the elderly or fixing a dispute, and move to something like that.

say: Ten years is almost a **normal career plan**, so fix it properly with training funds and wage support.
I'd treat it as a **debate**, not an emergency.
think: I'm mostly fine, a bit **uneasy**, because people say there's plenty of time and then do nothing.
By 2036 I'm 37, which is a long runway for a **qualification**.
do: Finish the care course slowly and aim for a **better-paid** care or clinic job by 2030.
Keep the supermarket job until a new one is **lined up**.
Move to a smaller, **cheaper** place with Dani.
feel: Mostly **calm** with a nag, like a leak she can't find.
S4.quote: Being good gets you a team lead badge, not a pension.
fieldNote: The long runway lowers distress, but she worries about her own **procrastination**.
Her advice to young colleagues shows she has accepted that till skill is **temporary**.
Wants **automatic** saving because she doesn't trust her own follow-through.

steps.text: Finish the care course at a slower pace and aim for a clinic job by 2030
Set up an automatic transfer toward six months of rent
Look for a smaller flat with cheaper rent with Dani

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years doesn't give me time to save or train, and it's the one where the firm can just say sorry and the government says it's a market matter. What would help is a proper cushion: a redundancy payment, paid study time and a job guarantee in care or something, written down before it's needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think cashiers don't think about this. We do. We stand in the front line of every new gadget, and we notice first when it doesn't work. Ask us before you buy the next one.

headlineQuote: We stand in the front line of every new gadget, and we notice first when it doesn't work.
portrait: Beth is 27, a **team lead** at a big supermarket, and the best till worker there, on lower pay.
She lives with Dani (her partner) and has about **two weeks** of savings, with few similar jobs nearby.
She never uses AI tools and trusts the **union** more than any manager's training video.
She blames owners and head office, not the machines, and wants **laws** on staffed tills and support.
Across the scenarios she moves from steady worry to alarm at 2028, and turns to **care training**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years gives no time to save or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A written **cushion**: redundancy pay, paid study time and a care-job guarantee.
Being **asked** before head office buys the next machine.
